desc:
Given an array nums of non-negative integers, count the pairs of positions i < j for which nums[i] + nums[j] is a power of two (that is, one of 1, 2, 4, 8, ...; note that 0 is not a power of two).

For example, nums = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9] gives 4, from the sums 1+3 = 4, 1+7 = 8, 3+5 = 8 and 7+9 = 16. For nums = [1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3, 7] the answer is 15.
hints: Checking every pair costs O(n<sup>2</sup>). How many different power-of-two values can a sum of two numbers below 2<sup>20</sup>+1 take?
At most 22 different ones: 20 up to 221. So for each element x there are only 22 partner values that could work, namely 2t - x.
Scan left to right with a hash map of counts of earlier values. For each x and each power p, add count[p - x] to the answer, then insert x.
editorial: Turn the question around: instead of testing every partner, enumerate the few sums that are allowed. Since each value is at most 220, a sum is at most 221, so the candidate sums are the 22 powers 20, ..., 221. For an element x the only partners that complete a good pair are the values p - x for these powers (a negative partner simply never exists).

Looking only at earlier elements counts each pair exactly once, including pairs of equal values such as 4 + 4 = 8. Different powers give different partner values, so nothing is counted twice for the same earlier element. Time is O(22 n), space O(n). The answer is at most C(10,000, 2), about 5·107.
